title: Competing Goals Are the Source of Many Group Conflicts
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece diagnoses a common source of team and board-level conflict that gets misattributed to personality or intelligence: unstated, competing end-state goals for a discussion. When group members implicitly disagree about the purpose of a conversation — differing on urgency, risk tolerance, or what "success" for the discussion even means — they talk past each other and draw uncharitable conclusions about one another. Using a board of directors reviewing financial performance as an extended example, the article shows how different unstated goals (accountability versus support versus root-cause analysis) generate conflict that looks personal but is actually structural. The prescribed fix is to explicitly agree on the end-state goal before engaging any important topic.
points: Conflict that looks like a personality or intelligence clash is often actually driven by group members holding unstated, competing goals for what the discussion should accomplish.

The board-of-directors example shows how different implicit goals for reviewing financial performance — accountability, support, root-cause analysis — generate real conflict without anyone intending it.
Group members with competing goals tend to draw uncharitable conclusions about each other (lazy, unintelligent, subversive) rather than recognizing the structural mismatch.
The prescribed fix is procedural: explicitly agree on the end-state goal or purpose of a discussion before engaging the topic itself, rather than assuming alignment.
quotes: Members of any group will engage in conflict when they have competing end-state goals or purposes for any discussion.
When members of any group are not after the same thing or disagree about the purpose of the discussion, they talk past each other.
After several discussions, group members draw negative conclusions about why others don’t seem to “get it,” often believing they are lazy, unintelligent, or highly subversive.
Somewhat surprisingly to some, Directors may have wildly different and competing goals for the purpose of the discussion or the end-state of financial oversight.
Different goals are rarely compatible and most often compete with one another.
Conflict in groups is inevitable, but combat between members is always optional.
